### 543. Tell the re-prompted dispatch to distrust the error count it inherited from the interrupting context
- **Effort**: low
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: Task 534

**Description**: Make the stall/strand re-prompt remedy tell the resuming dispatch that an error count inherited from the interrupting context is unverified and non-exhaustive. The remedy text today orders foreground re-verification but says nothing about the provenance of the failure count the resumer was handed, so a resumer that re-runs the build and then reconciles against the handed-down number can stop early believing it is done.

MEASURED. The interrupting context reported exactly one compile error in its uncommitted fragment (a type mismatch at a single line). The resuming instance, running the build itself, found eight -- all inside the same declaration, caused by `rw` leaving tuple projections unreduced inside the Rlad conjuncts. One reported, eight real, same fragment: the handed-down count was neither a floor that happened to be low nor a stale snapshot of a different state, it was a partial read of the same state. A resumer treating it as the error inventory would have fixed one site and declared the fragment clean.

WHY THE EXISTING TEXT DOES NOT ALREADY COVER THIS. Read the current remedy before editing; it is close enough that the gap is easy to misjudge. The doc's "Loop obligation" list carries four instructions, and item 2 already says to "Attribute each failure to its own edits or to pre-existing breakage, with `git log` / `git status` overlap evidence." That is an attribution obligation over the failures the resumer has in hand -- it presupposes an inventory and says how to apportion it. It does not say where the inventory comes from, does not forbid seeding it from the interrupting context, and does not say that a count arriving with the re-prompt carries no evidentiary weight. Item 1 orders the foreground re-run but stops at the re-run; nothing closes the loop by saying the re-run's own output is the sole inventory and the inherited count is discarded, not reconciled against.

ENUMERATE EVERY EMISSION SITE -- A FIX APPLIED TO ONE IS A FIX APPLIED TO NONE. `agent-system/extensions/core/scripts/orchestrate-cycle-postflight.sh` emits remedy prose at four sites, two per detector, and the script-side and doc-side wordings are read by different consumers:
  - the `stall_suspected` notice ("STALL SUSPECTED for task ... REMEDY: re-prompt this same dispatch ONCE, instructing it to re-run its verification in the FOREGROUND ...");
  - the `stall`-flavoured `recovery_declined_detail` ("RECORD-TIME CORROBORATION: ... commit(s) for this task landed inside the dispatch window ... REMEDY: one re-prompt, foreground verification, do NOT charge to failed_tasks without that re-prompt.");
  - the `stranded_suspected` notice ("STRAND SUSPECTED for task ...");
  - the `strand`-flavoured `recovery_declined_detail` ("dispatch-strand-probe.sh reports a stale heartbeat with a live holder pid ...").
Locate all four mechanically rather than trusting this list, and decide per site rather than globally. The two stall-flavoured sites MUST carry the addition: that detector fires precisely when work landed and the wrap-up did not, which is the case that produces an inherited partial count. The two strand-flavoured sites route into the identical one-re-prompt relay, so a resumer reaching them inherits the same hazard; if they are left unchanged, the completion summary must state why the asymmetry is correct rather than leaving it as an oversight. The two `recovery_declined_detail` sites are terse by construction and may carry a shorter form than the notices, provided the shorter form still says the count is not to be trusted.

DOC-SIDE TARGET. `agent-system/extensions/core/docs/architecture/orchestrate-state-machine.md`, section "Abandoned Wrap-Up: Re-Prompt Once Before Accepting a No-Outcome Verdict", subsection "Loop obligation". The four-item list there is the canonical statement the relay prompt is built from; the addition belongs in it, either as a new item or as a clause on item 1 that the re-run's output is the only inventory. Whichever shape is chosen, the script-side prose and the doc-side list must say the same thing -- a divergence between them is the defect this record exists to avoid reproducing.

SUBSTANCE OF THE ADDITION. Three things, stated as what the resumer does:

### 542. Record the launch-side PID-fidelity condition on the bounded-waiter detach form
- **Effort**: low
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: Task 538

**Description**: Record, in the core extension's bounded-waiter guidance, the launch-side condition that Rule 2 currently assumes but never states: the detach form must be one whose `$!` is the writer process itself. Rule 2 ("Writer liveness by captured PID, never by name") governs how liveness is TESTED and is explicit that a name-matching test is forbidden; it says nothing about how the writer is LAUNCHED, and therefore nothing about whether the PID it tells the caller to capture is in fact the writer's. A wrapper that forks between the shell and the writer satisfies Rule 2 to the letter and still produces a waiter that resolves immediately against a live writer.

NOTHING IN ANY SCRIPT IS BROKEN AND THIS IS NOT A DATA-REPAIR RECORD. The deliverable is guidance prose in the core extension's source store plus its index wiring. The canonical idiom at `## The Canonical Idiom` is already the correct direct form (`cmd >log 2>&1 & pid=$!`) and must not be rewritten; this record adds an explicit condition naming what that form is doing, so that a caller who substitutes a wrapper knows it is a substantive change rather than a cosmetic one.

=== THE MEASURED FAILURE ===

An implementation round detached `scripts/check-evidence-probes.sh` via a `setsid nohup ... &` form. Because `setsid` forks, `$!` captured the setsid wrapper rather than the guard, so the `kill -0` liveness loop saw its target exit almost immediately and reported the build finished while the guard was still running. The round recovered by polling the log for the guard's own terminal verdict line, and the guard did ultimately print its `PASS` verdict for all wired probes. Later detachments in the same round used a direct `bash script &` so that `$!` is the writer's own PID.

WHY IT MATTERS, AND WHY IT IS WORTH GUIDANCE AT ALL. This is a silent degradation of the idiom, not a loud failure. The waiter returns early, reports success, and whatever reads the log next sees a truncated or empty result that then gets interpreted as a real outcome. Every visible signal is a success signal. Contrast the name-matching failure already recorded in this file as symptom 3, which fails loudly by spinning forever and eventually drew an operator: that one announces itself, this one does not. A waiter that cannot tell "the writer finished" from "the wrapper I was watching exited" has lost the one property the idiom exists to provide.

=== THE DISCRIMINATION THE GUIDANCE MUST GET RIGHT, MEASURED ON THIS MACHINE ===

READ THIS BEFORE WRITING ANY PROSE. It is tempting to state the rule as "`setsid`/`nohup`-wrapped forms break PID capture." That is WRONG for `nohup`, and writing it would make the file contradict its own two correct examples. Measured directly, four detach forms of the same 4-second writer script, comparing the captured `$!` against the PID the writer printed for itself:

  (a) `bash ./w.sh >log 2>&1 & pid=$!`              -- captured PID == writer PID. `kill -0` correctly reports alive.
  (b) `nohup bash ./w.sh >log 2>&1 & pid=$!`        -- captured PID == writer PID. `kill -0` correctly reports alive.
  (c) `setsid nohup bash ./w.sh >log 2>&1 & pid=$!` -- captured PID is NOT the writer PID. `kill -0` fails within 1s while the writer runs on for 4 more seconds, then completes normally and writes its full output to the log.
  (d) `setsid bash ./w.sh >log 2>&1 & pid=$!`       -- captured PID is NOT the writer PID. Same early-exit failure as (c).

The mechanism, which the guidance should state rather than merely asserting a list of banned words: `nohup` `exec`s into the command and so is PID-transparent, while `setsid` forks a child to become a process-group leader and so interposes a process between the shell and the writer. `setsid` is the breaking wrapper in the measured incident; the `nohup` in that same command line was incidental. The rule to write is therefore a POSITIVE property with a test, not a blocklist: the detach form must be one whose `$!` is the writer itself, and any wrapper that forks rather than `exec`s violates it. State `setsid` as the known concrete instance and `nohup` as the known-safe contrast, because a reader who has just been told "wrappers are dangerous" will otherwise go looking for the `nohup` forms in this very file and break them.

=== TWO PASSAGES THAT MUST NOT BE EDITED ===

Both are measured-correct under (b) above, and an implementer who reads the new rule as anti-`nohup` will be drawn to both. They stay exactly as they are:

  1. In `## The Defect`, symptom 3's quoted incident command, which begins `nohup timeout 3000 ... check.sh > log 2>&1 & disown`. This is a verbatim quote of a historical non-conforming command, non-conforming for its name-matching poll, NOT for its `nohup`. Rewriting a quoted incident to match a later rule destroys the evidence the passage exists to carry.
  2. In `## Conforming Examples`, the generic gate-script entry `nohup timeout 3000 bash gate.sh >log 2>&1 & pid=$!`. This remains conforming. If the new condition were written as anti-`nohup`, this example would have to be edited to stay consistent -- and that pressure is the signal the rule was written wrong, not that the example is wrong.

=== HARD SCOPE BOUNDARY: DO NOT TOUCH THE GENERATED-COPY CONTRACT BULLET ===

The file's `## Canonical Agent-Contract Bullet (Generated-Copy Source)` section is the single authoritative source for a MUST / MUST NOT bullet pair whose MUST half reads in part "a captured `pid=$!`, a `kill -0` liveness loop, and an outer `timeout N`". MEASURED: that bullet text appears verbatim in 27 agent files across 14 extensions, and `lint-agent-contracts.sh` Check H keeps every copy byte-identical by comparing against this file. Verify with a grep for the literal string `bounded-build-waiter.md's canonical idiom VERBATIM` across the source store.

Consequently: adding the detach-form condition to that bullet converts a one-file prose change into a 28-file synchronized edit gated by a lint check. DO NOT DO IT. The bullet already binds its carriers to the canonical idiom "VERBATIM" and so already inherits whatever the idiom section says; the new condition belongs in the Required Rules prose, where a reader who follows the bullet's own pointer will meet it. If research concludes the bullet genuinely must change, RAISE IT rather than executing a 28-file edit under a record scoped and sized as a single-file guidance change.

=== THE SECOND NAMED FILE IS A CROSS-REFERENCE, NOT A SECOND HOME ===

The change request named `context/patterns/external-process-wait.md` as a place that "states the same idiom." MEASURED: it does not. That file contains ZERO detach-launch forms -- no `& pid=$!` line anywhere in it -- and mentions `kill -0` exactly twice, both times as a cross-reference pointing at the bounded-waiter file (once in its sub-case 3b remedy, once in its `## Local vs. Remote Waits` section, which states explicitly that it covers the case where "there is no local writer to probe" and directs the local detached case to the other file). Its subject is a polled remote status with no local PID at all, so a launch-side PID-fidelity rule has no work to do there.

The correct action for that file is therefore NOTHING, or at most leaving its existing cross-references untouched because they already resolve to the amended rule. DO NOT restate the condition there: the bounded-waiter file's own `### Item 1 Ruling: One Shared Home, Rejected Candidates Recorded` section establishes the single-home principle for exactly this idiom, and a second copy in a file whose scope excludes local writers would be both redundant and wrong in its own context. If the implementer judges a pointer sentence genuinely adds navigational value, it may be added as one sentence that points, never one that restates -- and `external-process-wait.md`'s `line_count` in `index-entries.json` must then be updated with it.

=== AN ADJACENCY RAISED, DELIBERATELY NOT FOLDED IN ===

`hooks/validate-bounded-waiter.sh` is a PreToolUse hook that BLOCKS the name-matching waiter shape via a three-leg conjunction (a loop keyword, a delay call, and a process-name-matching liveness test). It does not detect the forking-wrapper shape, and cannot: the shape has no name-matching leg. That hook's own header argues that for this family "documentation-as-prohibition had already failed for this exact command shape, which is why this hook exists: mechanical teeth, not a sixth restatement."

That argument plainly bears on the present record, which IS a documentation change for a sibling failure in the same family. It is named here so a future reader does not mistake its absence for an oversight. It is NOT in scope: the approved change request is guidance-only, a hook leg for this shape is a separate design question (what is the safe conjunction? a bare `setsid` is legitimate in other contexts, so a one-leg match would be a false-positive machine of exactly the kind that hook's header forbids), and the two have different blast radii. Whoever executes this record should state in its completion summary whether the mechanical backstop is worth proposing as a follow-up, rather than quietly adding a hook leg.

A FURTHER MEASURED PROPERTY OF THAT HOOK, RECORDED HERE AS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN AS SCOPE. The hook matches the raw command TEXT, which includes heredoc payloads. During the creation of this record, an attempt to write this very description into a file via a `cat <<'EOF'` heredoc was BLOCKED by the hook, because the description's own prose about the forbidden shape supplied all three legs of the conjunction. Writing documentation about the banned shape is therefore itself blocked by the guard protecting that shape, and the workaround was to write the file with a non-Bash file-writing tool. This is a real false-positive class, it will recur for anyone editing this family of guidance, and it is NOT part of this record's deliverable -- it is reported separately to the dispatching lead for triage. It is noted here only because a future implementer of THIS record will very likely hit it while editing these same files, and should reach for a non-Bash write rather than concluding their edit is malformed.

=== FOLDED-IN CHANGE REQUEST: THE PID MUST CROSS THE BASH-CALL BOUNDARY ===

Folded into this record by /orchestrate's conclusion stage (agent-system channel) during session
`sess_1793842874_bc66e8`, originating task 855, issue entry_id `iss_1793844057182_bHlVYf`, class
`tooling-friction`, severity `minor`. Folded here rather than filed as a fourth claimant because
this record already owns both edit targets in its `file_scope`
(`agent-system/extensions/core/context/patterns/bounded-build-waiter.md` and
`agent-system/extensions/core/index-entries.json`), is unstarted, and its subject IS the
launch-side fidelity of the captured PID. The addition below is the same `$!` capture followed one
step further: across a Bash-call boundary.

THE GAP, MEASURED BY READING THE FILE. `bounded-build-waiter.md`'s
`### Sizing a Wait Near the Per-Call Ceiling` section already prescribes the multi-call form in
full -- "launch once, capturing `pid`, then issue a *sequence* of separate bounded calls, each
gated on `kill -0 "$pid"` and sized safely under the ceiling" -- and `external-process-wait.md`
Rule 1's sub-case 3b already redirects to it by name. So the SEQUENCE rule is not missing and must
not be re-derived or restated. What is missing is the one mechanical step that makes the sequence
executable: HOW `$pid` reaches the second call. Bash-tool shell state does not persist across
calls, so a `pid=$!` captured in the launching call is simply gone by the next one, and the
section's own `kill -0 "$pid"` is unresolvable as literally written for any caller who follows it
across a real call boundary. The fix is to state the persistence step: redirect the writer's
stdout to a log, write `$!` to a PID file in the same command, and in each following call re-read
the PID from that file before the `kill -0` loop.

THE PRECEDENT IS ALREADY IN-TREE AND IS THE MODEL TO CITE. `skills/skill-orchestrate/SKILL.md`
Move 1 already implements exactly this, conformingly:

  nohup bash .claude/scripts/orchestrate-cycle-plan.sh ... >"$cycle_log" & echo $! > "$cycle_log.pid"
  pid=$(cat "$cycle_log.pid")
  timeout 540 bash -c 'while kill -0 "$1" 2>/dev/null; do sleep 10; done' _ "$pid"

and that file's Move 3 names it a reusable idiom ("Same nohup/pid-capture/bounded-kill-0 idiom").
Note for consistency with this record's own four-form measurement: that form's `nohup` is
PID-transparent (form (b)), so `echo $!` writes the writer's own PID to the file and the form is
correct. This is also why the two subjects belong in one record -- a PID file is only as good as
the `$!` that fed it, and a forking wrapper (form (c)/(d)) poisons the file just as it poisons an
in-shell `pid` variable, except that the PID file makes the wrong value durable and re-read on
every subsequent call.

=== A CLAIM IN THE CHANGE REQUEST THAT MUST NOT BE PROPAGATED: THERE IS NO 180s THRESHOLD ===

READ THIS BEFORE WRITING ANY PROSE. The originating issue entry states the gate "exceeds the Bash
tool's 180s auto-background threshold." MEASURED: that threshold does not exist. `grep` for
`180s` across the entire source store returns NOTHING, and the documented contract -- stated in
`external-process-wait.md` Rule 1 step (2) and again in this file's own canonical-idiom section --
is a Bash-tool `timeout` parameter DEFAULTING to `120000`ms (120s) with a CEILING of `600000`ms
(600s). The harness auto-backgrounds at whatever that parameter is set to, so the operative number
is 120s when the caller leaves the default alone and 600s when the caller raises it. 180 is
neither.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS SUBSTANTIVE, NOT PEDANTIC. The originating gate runs roughly 5 minutes (~300s).
That FITS under the 600s ceiling, so it is sub-case 3a in `external-process-wait.md` Rule 1's
terms -- "raising the parameter is sufficient" -- and is correctly resolved by ONE bounded
foreground call with the tool `timeout` parameter raised to `600000`, not by the two-call form at
all. The friction recorded in the originating entry is therefore best explained as the tool
`timeout` parameter being left at its `120000` default, which is precisely the failure step (2) of
that rule exists to prevent. The two-call sequence genuinely IS required only for a job that
cannot fit under 600s even once sized (sub-case 3b).

SO DO NOT WRITE THIS AS A THRESHOLD RULE. Specifically, the guidance MUST NOT say, in any phrasing,
that a gate exceeding some fixed number of seconds needs the multi-call form. That would (i)
enshrine a number the harness does not implement, (ii) contradict this file's and
`external-process-wait.md`'s own 120/600 arithmetic, and (iii) push callers toward the strictly
more complex detached form for jobs a single raised-parameter call handles correctly, which
inverts the canonical-idiom section's standing preference for the simpler foreground form. State
the PID-persistence step as a property of the multi-call sequence WHEREVER that sequence is
already warranted -- i.e. governed by the existing 3a/3b split -- and let the existing sub-case
split keep deciding when it is warranted.

=== THE "GATES VERSUS BUILDS" FRAMING IS ALSO NOT A REAL GAP ===

The change request argued the sequence rule is stated for long-running BUILDS but not for
long-running GATES. MEASURED: the section is already job-generic -- it opens on "A job whose
expected duration approaches the Bash tool's own per-call ceiling," and its second paragraph
explicitly names "a local verification/gate/build/test process." Gates are already inside its
scope. Do NOT add a gates-specific carve-out, a parallel gate paragraph, or a restatement scoped
to gates; that would create exactly the kind of second home this file's
`### Item 1 Ruling: One Shared Home, Rejected Candidates Recorded` section forbids. The addition
is one mechanism (PID persistence), not a new audience.

  - `external-process-wait.md` carries no restatement. Its sub-case 3b already points here by

### 541. Stop git-snapshot.sh --no-revert artifacts from contaminating phase commits with other tasks files
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: Task 535

**Description**: Stop git-snapshot.sh's --no-revert artifacts from contaminating phase commits with OTHER tasks' files. Two cooperating defects, one in each script; fix the pair, because fixing either alone leaves the contamination reachable.

MEASURED EVIDENCE -- RE-DERIVABLE, DO NOT RE-DERIVE FROM SCRATCH. Commit `b7bba072e` ("task 744 phase 2: wrap RaySummary and KTypeSummary with targeted regeneration") contains 13 files belonging to FOUR unrelated tasks, copied under `specs/744_wrap_inventory_tables_generated_markers/untracked-backup-1792263067/specs/`: `566_possible_worlds_clause_hf_as_limit`, `616_duration_monoid_twisted_arrow_interval_site`, `617_reflection_clause_converse_frame_naturality`, and `785_lean_plan_gate_collision_authoring_guidance`. Verify with `git show --name-only b7bba072e | grep untracked-backup`. Those four directories are STILL untracked in the working tree today, so the repository now carries committed copies of files their owners deliberately left untracked, under a fifth task's directory. They were removed by hand with `git rm` in the phase 3 commit.

DEFECT HALF 1 -- UNSCOPED ENUMERATION, AND THE PLACEMENT THAT EXPOSES IT. In `scripts/git-snapshot.sh`, `--no-revert` mode enumerates untracked files with a bare, REPOSITORY-WIDE `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` and copies every hit to `UNTRACKED_BACKUP="${TASK_DIR}/untracked-backup-${TS}"`. The enumeration is not filtered by the dispatching task's declared `file_scope`, nor by anything else. The sibling `PATCH_PATH="${TASK_DIR}/working-progress-${TS}.patch"` lands in the same place. Both therefore sit INSIDE the dispatching task's own specs directory, which is precisely the directory the phase-commit wrapper stages wholesale.

DEFECT HALF 2 -- THE DIRECTORY PATHSPEC THAT SWEEPS THEM IN, AND WHY NOTHING WARNED. In `scripts/git-commit-phase.sh` the fixed scope is `stage_paths=("${task_dir}/" "specs/TODO.md" "specs/state.json")`, a DIRECTORY pathspec staged first and unconditionally. The script's own header declares this fixed scope "never tested by the Containment Self-Check", so anything sitting in the task directory at commit time is staged with no containment test, no warning, and no `issues.jsonl` entry. That is why the contamination was silent. Note the standing tension with `.claude/rules/git-workflow.md`, which forbids a directory-or-glob `git add` pathspec precisely because it "silently pull[s] in concurrent-session or unrelated edits" -- this is that failure, arriving through the wrapper's fixed scope rather than through a hand-typed `git add`.

THE COST IS A SURRENDERED SAFETY MECHANISM, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN NOTING. After reverting the contamination, the implementer stopped taking snapshots for the remaining phases to avoid recurrence. The workaround was to give up the defensive checkpoint. `context/patterns/checkpoint-before-overflow.md` sanctions `--no-revert` as the ordinary defensive checkpoint, and `.claude/rules/git-workflow.md` directs agents to prefer it over the reverting default for exactly this purpose; the defect makes that sanctioned pattern unsafe to use inside any phase-committing dispatch.

RECURRENCE -- BROADER THAN THE ONE CITED COMMIT. `git log --all -- 'specs/*/working-progress-*.patch'` shows the patch half landing in commits across tasks 744, 807, 805 and 794, and `git ls-files 'specs/*/working-progress-*.patch'` shows one still tracked today (under `807_backward_determinism_forcing_check`). The patch sweep is routine, not exceptional. The foreign-file sweep additionally requires foreign untracked files to be present at snapshot time, which is common during multi-task work but not universal.

DESIGN TENSION THAT MUST BE RESOLVED EXPLICITLY, NOT ASSUMED AWAY. The obvious relocation target is the ephemeral gitignored runtime-file class (`specs/.gitignore` carries `**/.orchestration/`, confirmed; the class and its 19 registered members are specified in `context/standards/orchestrator-runtime-files.md`, with patterns in `scripts/lib/runtime-file-patterns.sh` and reaping in `scripts/reap-session-runtime-files.sh`). But `git-snapshot.sh`'s own header states a DELIBERATE contrary property: "the marker filename is gitignored (**/.git-snapshot-marker); the durable working-progress-*.patch file is NOT gitignored and remains tracked under the task directory for manual recovery if needed." Relocating the patch into the ephemeral class would convert a deliberately-durable, tracked recovery artifact into an untracked one subject to `reap-session-runtime-files.sh` deletion after `ORCHESTRATOR_SESSION_REAP_MIN`. Decide this on the merits and record the reasoning; do not treat the `.orchestration/` candidate as pre-approved. The two artifacts may warrant DIFFERENT answers -- the untracked-backup copies are duplicates of files that are themselves untracked (so making them ephemeral costs little), whereas the patch is the primary durable record of tracked-change state. If the patch stays tracked where it is, then Half 2's exclusion stops being a second line of defense and becomes the whole defense for that artifact, which raises its priority accordingly.

QUESTIONS TO SETTLE, IN THIS ORDER.
  (1) Should the untracked backup be scoped to the dispatching task's declared `file_scope` rather than the whole repository? Weigh honestly against the snapshot's stated purpose: `--no-revert` currently reverts nothing, so a narrower backup loses no safety for THIS task, but the default and `--branch` modes DO revert via `git stash push -u`, which sweeps untracked files repository-wide -- so for those modes a repo-wide backup is arguably correct and narrowing it would lose data. Check whether the enumeration is shared across modes before narrowing it in a way that only suits one. Also define the behavior when `file_scope` is absent (many non-terminal tasks declare none) and do not silently fall back to repo-wide copying without saying so.
  (2) Where do the artifacts belong so a directory pathspec cannot reach them? Resolve the durability tension above.
  (3) Does `git-commit-phase.sh`'s fixed-scope pathspec need an explicit exclusion (e.g. a `:(exclude)` magic pathspec for the snapshot artifact names) as a line of defense independent of where the artifacts land? Prefer belt-and-suspenders here given that (2) may leave the patch in place.

ACCEPTANCE -- THE REGRESSION CHECK IS THE DELIVERABLE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT. Add a case to `scripts/tests/test-git-commit-phase.sh` and/or `scripts/tests/test-git-snapshot.sh` (both exist in the source store; extend them, do not replace existing cases) that fixtures a repository with foreign untracked `specs/` directories present, runs a `--no-revert` snapshot for one task, then runs that task's phase commit, and asserts NO foreign path is staged or committed. Demonstrate the new case FAILS against the unmodified scripts before the fix lands -- the suites are green while the defect is live, so a case that cannot fail first proves nothing. Then redeploy via `bash .claude/scripts/deploy-headless.sh` and confirm `RESULT=landed_verify_clean`.

NON-GOALS. No retroactive history rewrite to purge the already-committed foreign copies from `b7bba072e` (history rewrites are barred while other writers are live; see `.claude/rules/git-workflow.md`). Removing the one still-tracked patch under `807_backward_determinism_forcing_check` is optional cleanup, not required. No change to the guard-hook marker protocol, the single-shot marker consumption, or `git-snapshot.sh`'s stash-identity scheme. No change to `git-commit-scoped.sh` or its V-gate exit-code contract -- both halves sit one layer above it. No change to the containment predicate's treatment of GENUINE out-of-scope paths.

RELATIONSHIP TO THE ADJACENT PHASE-COMMIT RECORD. Task 777 (`phase_commit_drops_own_plan_artifact`) concerns the OPPOSITE direction of the same wrapper: its containment filter false-positively DROPS a task's own plan artifact. This record concerns the fixed-scope pathspec OVER-staging foreign files. They are distinct defects at distinct sites in one file -- 777 edits `is_contained()`, this edits the `stage_paths` construction -- but they share `scripts/git-commit-phase.sh`, `scripts/tests/test-git-commit-phase.sh`, and `context/standards/git-staging-scope.md`, so this record declares a dependency on 777 and runs after it rather than concurrently. 777 also corrects a false premise sentence in `git-staging-scope.md` about the fixed scope being "structurally outside [the filter's] reach"; read the CORRECTED text before editing that standard here, and do not reintroduce or re-correct that sentence.

SOURCE-STORE BOUNDARY. `.claude/**` is a gitignored, regenerated deploy artifact; a hand edit there is silently wiped by the next deploy and will appear to succeed while having no lasting effect. The owning extension is `core`, whose `source_dir` resolves from `<project-root>/.claude-extensions.json` to `/home/benjamin/.config/nvim/agent-system/extensions/core`. Edit at the mirroring paths there -- `scripts/git-snapshot.sh`, `scripts/git-commit-phase.sh`, the two test suites, and any of `context/patterns/checkpoint-before-overflow.md`, `context/standards/orchestrator-runtime-files.md`, `context/standards/git-staging-scope.md`, `scripts/lib/runtime-file-patterns.sh` the chosen fix touches -- per `.claude/rules/source-store-deploy-boundary.md`, then redeploy. The `.claude/**` paths in `file_scope` are declared only so the admission overlap gate can see the collision surface; they are NOT the edit target.

DELIVERABLE HYGIENE. Every edited file is outside `specs/**`, so its prose must carry no task-number references (`.claude/rules/no-task-references-in-deliverables.md`) and no record-versioning language (`.claude/rules/no-record-versioning-in-deliverables.md`). Cite durable anchors only -- file names, variable names (`UNTRACKED_BACKUP`, `PATCH_PATH`, `stage_paths`, `TASK_DIR`), flag names (`--no-revert`), and section headings.

PROVENANCE AND CITATION. Raised by /orchestrate's conclusion stage, channel (b) agent-system changes, user-approved for session `sess_1792261594_b3e099` (approval ledger `specs/.orchestration/.conclusion-approval-sess_1792261594_b3e099.json`, channel b = yes). The originating issue-log entry is `entry_id: iss_1792263251358_jTp86B` in `specs/744_wrap_inventory_tables_generated_markers/issues.jsonl` -- `class: tooling`, `severity: minor`, `resolution: null`. Read that entry verbatim before composing anything. The `minor` severity is correct for data loss (nothing was lost; the foreign files were copies, and the originals remain untracked in place) but understates the mechanism: the defect writes other tasks' files into a commit silently, and the observed mitigation was to abandon the snapshot safety net for the rest of the run.

### 540. Record the decide-synthesis working form, the axiom-free maxRecDepth remedy, and the probe guard's total arithmetic
- **Effort**: low
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: Task 539

**Description**: Record three measured Lean authoring and probe-guard facts from one evidence-probe implementation round: the working form for a `Decidable` instance under nested `Finset` binders, the axiom-free `set_option maxRecDepth` remedy and its first precedent in this probe collection, and the arithmetic behind the evidence-probe guard's printed probe total.

NOTHING IS BROKEN AND THIS IS NOT A DATA-REPAIR RECORD. All three facts were measured during one implementation round and all three were already handled in that round: the synthesis failure was resolved in the probe source, the recursion budget was raised in the probe file, and the off-by-one was in a plan's predicted output rather than in the guard. `scripts/check-evidence-probes.sh` is CORRECT as it stands -- its total is right and the prediction was wrong -- so do NOT change the script, its arrays, or any probe file. This record's entire deliverable is prose plus index wiring.

=== ITEM A -- `Decidable` SYNTHESIS UNDER NESTED Finset BINDERS (the first thing an implementer hits) ===

MEASURED. The first compile of a pinned Challenge block failed on exactly one `Decidable` synthesis. The box clause, written as a nested iff under two `Finset` binders, would not synthesize:

    decide (forall x in R, forall psi in closure, isBox psi -> (psi in x.2.1 <-> forall y in R, argOf psi in y.2.1))

Two changes resolved it and recompiled to exit 0: pushing the INNER universal into its own `decide` and comparing `Bool`s rather than leaving it inside the iff, and factoring the stab clause into a named `stabOk` helper rather than inlining it.

THE DURABLE LESSON TO RECORD. Capture the WORKING FORM, not merely the failure: a decidable clause of the shape "for every element of a Finset, a membership test iff a further Finset-quantified membership test" should be written with the inner quantifier decided separately and the two `Bool`s compared, and a multi-clause structure predicate should factor each clause into a named helper. The guidance should say WHY this is worth pre-empting rather than discovering: this shape is the first thing an implementer meets on the `stab`/`box` fields of a structure predicate over a closure, so a plan that pins such a predicate should pin the working form rather than the natural-looking nested-iff form.

=== ITEM B -- `set_option maxRecDepth` IS AXIOM-FREE, AND IS NOW PRECEDENTED HERE ===

MEASURED. Six component `decide`s of one certificate acceptance theorem (`certLoc`/`certBiInf`/`certFwd`/`certBwd`/`certStab`/`certBox` over a three-element candidate relation) all overran the default `maxRecDepth` of 512. The carrier was never enumerated -- the anticipated "`decide` over a 2^18 x 8 space" hazard did not fire at all; this was purely a kernel stack budget on reducing a closure literal and its membership tests. The remedy was a file-level `set_option maxRecDepth 20000` carrying a comment recording that it adds no axiom.

THE DURABLE LESSON TO RECORD, in two parts:

  - `set_option maxRecDepth <n>` is an AXIOM-FREE remedy: it raises an elaboration/kernel recursion budget and adds nothing to a declaration's axiom set, UNLIKE `native_decide`, which does. The contrast with `native_decide` is the load-bearing part and should be stated explicitly, because the two look like interchangeable "make `decide` finish" moves and are not: one is free, the other changes what the result certifies.
  - The hazard it addresses is DISTINCT from search-space size. A budget overrun on reducing a literal and its membership tests can fire even when the carrier is never enumerated, so a plan that has ruled out the large-search-space hazard has NOT thereby ruled out this one. Before this round no probe in the collection had a `maxRecDepth` precedent; it now has one, which is worth saying so a later author treats the option as established practice in this collection rather than a novel escape hatch.

A PLACEMENT NOTE, to check before writing: `context/project/lean4/domain/lean4-syntax.md` already mentions `set_option maxRecDepth` -- but only in the narrow context of where a docstring may sit relative to a `set_option ... in` prefix, which is a different subject. Decide whether item B lands in `patterns/tactic-patterns.md` beside the `### decide` material or beside that existing mention, and do not leave two divergent statements of the same fact in the two files; a pointer from one to the other is preferable to a second copy.

=== ITEM C -- THE EVIDENCE-PROBE GUARD'S PRINTED TOTAL IS THE SUM OF TWO ARRAYS ===

MEASURED. A phase's Scope Hypothesis predicted that the `WIRED` array in `scripts/check-evidence-probes.sh` would go from 37 to 38 entries (CONFIRMED by measurement) and inferred that the guard would therefore report "all 38 wired probe(s) compile". It reports "all 39": the script computes `wired_total` as `WIRED` plus the one-entry `WIRED_REPO` array (the archived fmp-hypothesis probe, cited by its task-directory path). The array figures were exactly as predicted; only the derived printed total was wrong, by exactly the size of `WIRED_REPO`.

THE DURABLE LESSON TO RECORD. State that the guard's printed "all N wired probe(s) compile" total is the SUM of the `WIRED` and `WIRED_REPO` arrays, so a prediction of the printed total from the `WIRED` count alone is short by the size of `WIRED_REPO`. Verify the current `WIRED_REPO` size against the script rather than carrying the figure from this record, and prefer stating the relationship (sum of both arrays) over any particular numbers, which drift as probes are added.

A SITING NOTE FOR THIS ITEM, which differs from A and B. The script is this repository's own (`scripts/check-evidence-probes.sh`), not an agent-system file, and `scripts/README.md` already carries a one-row description of it -- extending that row is the smallest edit that puts the fact where a reader of the script will find it, and it is an ORDINARY REPOSITORY EDIT with no source-store boundary implication. The alternative home is a lean-extension context file, serving the plan author who writes a Scope Hypothesis about the guard's output; `context/patterns/task-abandon-mode.md` and `skills/skill-todo/SKILL.md` already mention the `WIRED_REPO` form for a different purpose (re-pointing a guard that cites a file by its task-directory path) and are NOT the right home for counting semantics. Both candidate paths are in `file_scope`; choose one, or state the fact in the repository row and add a pointer from the lean side. If a third path is chosen, widen `file_scope` first.

=== WHY ONE RECORD RATHER THAN THREE ===

All three facts come from the same implementation round, all three are one-to-three-sentence additions to files that already exist, and each alone is far too small to carry a record's overhead. A and B share a single edit surface (the `### decide` material in `patterns/tactic-patterns.md`) and would collide there if filed separately with nothing to serialize them. C has a different edit surface and no overlap with A or B, but is a single clause. The guidance must state the three as three separately checkable facts, not blur them into one "watch out for `decide`" paragraph.

=== DEPENDENCY ===

This record depends on the lean plan-authoring Challenge-block contract record (task 813), for a mechanical reason: both edit the lean extension's `index-entries.json` (813 updates `challenge-snapshot.md`'s `line_count`, this record updates `tactic-patterns.md`'s), and an unordered overlap on that file is exactly the collision a dependency edge exists to serialize. There is no logical dependency between the two bodies of guidance.

=== SOURCE-STORE BOUNDARY, AND ITS RESOLUTION STEP ===

Items A and B are agent-system edits. `.claude/**` in this repository is a gitignored, regenerated deploy artifact: a hand edit there is wiped by the next deploy and will appear to succeed while having no lasting effect (`.claude/rules/source-store-deploy-boundary.md`). Those edits land in the source store at the path mirroring the deployed one, never under `.claude/**`.

RESOLVE THE SOURCE STORE BEFORE EDITING, AND DO NOT ASSUME A PATH. This repository's `<project-root>/.claude-extensions.json` has NO `source_dir` key at all -- its only top-level keys are `extensions` and `version` -- so the documented resolution step does not yield a path here. The convention adjacent records use, and which is present on this machine, is `/home/benjamin/.config/nvim/agent-system/extensions/lean`; confirm it holds before writing, and if the source store is unreachable or ambiguous, REPORT THAT AND STOP rather than falling back to editing the deploy tree. The owning extension for both agent-system paths in `file_scope` is `lean`, not `core`.

### 539. State the precedence and snapshot-prerequisite rules for a lean plan's pinned Challenge block
- **Effort**: low
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: None

**Description**: Close two plan-authoring contract gaps that a lean plan's pinned `## Lean Challenge Statements` block makes possible: that a plan may state a Verification criterion contradicting its own pinned block, and that a plan may name `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh --check` in a phase's Verification without ever scheduling the snapshot that check requires.

NOTHING IN EITHER REPOSITORY IS BROKEN, AND THIS IS NOT A DATA-REPAIR RECORD. Both gaps were observed during one implementation run and both were resolved inside that run -- the contradiction was resolved in favour of the pinned Challenge order, and the unrunnable advisory check was replaced by a stronger self-contained substitute. `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh`, `plan-compliance.md`, `plan-format.md` and the originating probe are all correct as they stand; do not re-edit the script and do not change its exit-code behaviour. This record's entire deliverable is plan-authoring prose plus its index wiring.

=== ITEM 1 -- A VERIFICATION CRITERION THAT CONTRADICTS THE PLAN'S OWN PINNED BLOCK ===

MEASURED. A plan's Phase 4 Verification required that `cert_accepts_Rchi` precede every theorem whose statement is a negation or an inequality, "checked by line number". That same plan's pinned `## Lean Challenge Statements` block itself ordered two negative statements BEFORE `cert_accepts_Rchi`: an inequality (`au_lfp_ne_eu_lfp_on_exit_graph`) and a `= false` conjunction (`chi_closure_box_snce_stab_free`). The two instructions could not both be satisfied. The implementer resolved it in favour of the pinned Challenge order, on the ground that Statement Fidelity governs the contract, and honoured the non-vacuity-before-negation discipline for every negative statement ABOUT the certificate and the candidate sets (`rev_eu_lfp_empty`, `cert_rejects_Rev`, `profR_separates_gate6_pair`), all of which follow `cert_accepts_Rchi`.

THE DURABLE LESSON TO RECORD, as two separately checkable conditions:

  (a) A PRECEDENCE RULE for the divergence case: when a plan's own Verification prose and its pinned `## Lean Challenge Statements` block disagree about declaration order (or about anything else the block fixes), the pinned block wins. The reason is mechanical rather than stylistic and the guidance should give it: the block is pinned before implementation and is immutable by design thereafter -- `plan-compliance.md`'s Statement Fidelity section already forbids quietly editing a recorded Challenge to match what was implemented -- whereas a Verification criterion is ordinary plan prose. An implementer who resolves such a divergence the other way has silently edited the contract.

  (b) AN AUTHORING PROHIBITION, so the divergence is not created in the first place: a plan author who pins a Challenge block MUST NOT then write an order-dependent Verification criterion (a "precedes", "follows", or "checked by line number" criterion) whose required order differs from the order of declarations in that block. The block is the order of record; a criterion restating it adds nothing and a criterion contradicting it is unsatisfiable as written.

The guidance should also say what an implementer does when it happens anyway, since this gap cannot be fully closed by authoring discipline alone: resolve in favour of the pinned block, and record the divergence rather than silently choosing. That is what the measured run did.

=== ITEM 2 -- `--check` NAMED IN A PHASE THAT HAS NO MANIFEST TO CHECK AGAINST ===

MEASURED. A plan's Phase 6 Verification named `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh --check {N} .` as an advisory step. The plan round had pinned its Challenge block in the plan file but had never taken a snapshot, so no manifest existed and the script exited 71 with "no manifest found at specs/{NNN}_{SLUG}/challenge/manifest.json -- run the snapshot (without --check) first". The criterion was therefore unmeetable exactly as written. The implementer substituted a stronger, self-contained check: a mechanical declaration-by-declaration diff of the probe against the plan's own `## Lean Challenge Statements` block, reporting every declaration present and zero signature mismatches. Because `--check` is advisory-only (`plan-compliance.md`, "Mechanical check"; `challenge-snapshot.md`, "Gate Strength: Advisory Only"), the substitution did not affect `verification_passed`.

THE DURABLE LESSON TO RECORD. Pinning a Challenge block in a plan file and taking a Challenge snapshot are two different acts, and only the second produces the manifest `--check` reads. State the rule in both directions so a plan author can satisfy it either way:

  - If any phase's Verification names `--check`, an earlier step in the same plan MUST run `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh` WITHOUT `--check` to create the manifest. That snapshot is an explicit plan step, not something the pinned block causes to happen.
  - Otherwise the plan MUST NOT name `--check` at all. A criterion naming a check that cannot run is not an advisory check, it is dead prose.

The guidance should also record the sanctioned fallback, since a plan that pins a block but takes no snapshot still has a verifiable statement contract: a declaration-by-declaration diff of the implemented declarations against the plan's own pinned block is a legitimate self-contained substitute for `--check`, with the same advisory standing.

=== ITEM 3 -- ITEM 2'S FIRST REMEDY BRANCH IS UNATTAINABLE AS WRITTEN: A PLAN STEP CANNOT TAKE THE SNAPSHOT AT ALL ===

THIS ITEM CORRECTS ITEM 2 AND MUST BE LANDED WITH IT, NOT AFTER IT. Item 2 above states the rule in two branches: either an earlier step in the same plan runs `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh` without `--check` to create the manifest, or the plan must not name `--check` at all. The SECOND branch is correct and unaffected. The FIRST branch cannot be satisfied by any step of an implementation plan, and writing it as though it can would land guidance that sends the next plan author into exactly the dead end measured below.

MEASURED, in a second, later run. A plan's Phase 1 task list contained, verbatim, the step item 2's first branch prescribes -- take the snapshot so that `--check` is available to later phases, scheduled as the earliest task of the earliest phase. It REFUSED with exit 73: "snapshot refused -- task {N}'s status is 'implementing' (past 'planned')". The plan had done precisely what item 2's first branch asks and the step was still unreachable.

THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL AND MECHANICAL, NOT A TUNING ACCIDENT. `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh` admits only the pre-implementation statuses -- `not_started`, `researching`, `researched`, `planning`, `planned` -- without `--force`, and refuses anything past them with exit 73, on the stated ground that a Challenge must predate implementation to certify anything. By the time ANY phase of an implementation plan executes, the task's status has already advanced to `implementing`. So the set of plan steps that can take a snapshot is empty by construction: "an earlier step in the same plan" is unreachable for every plan, in every phase, including the first task of Phase 1. No plan-authoring discipline can repair this, because the obstruction is the status gate, not the plan's ordering.

THE IMPLEMENTER DID NOT FORCE IT, AND THAT WAS RIGHT. `--force` exists and would have produced a manifest. It was not used, on the ground the tool's own incident banner states: a Challenge produced after implementation has started certifies nothing about what the implementation agent actually saw, so a forced manifest would have committed misleading provenance into git history to satisfy an advisory check. Record this as the sanctioned behaviour: an implementer meeting a plan-scheduled snapshot step that the status gate refuses MUST NOT reach for `--force`, and falls back to item 2's sanctioned self-contained substitute (the declaration-by-declaration diff against the plan's own pinned block) instead. That is what the measured run did.

THE CORRECTED RULE TO WRITE. The act of taking a Challenge snapshot belongs to the PLAN phase, not to the implementation plan: it must happen while the task's status is still `planning` or `planned` -- by the planner, or in plan postflight -- and it is therefore an obligation on whoever produces the plan, never a task inside it. Restate item 2's branches accordingly:

  - If any phase's Verification names `--check`, the snapshot MUST already have been taken before the plan's status leaves `planned`. State it as a plan-phase obligation of the plan's author, and do not describe it as a step the plan schedules for the implementer.
  - Otherwise the plan MUST NOT name `--check` at all. (Unchanged from item 2.)
  - A plan that schedules the snapshot as one of its own phase tasks is DEFECTIVE, and the guidance should say so explicitly with the exit code, so a reader who meets exit 73 recognises it as this defect rather than as a broken tool.

WHETHER THE PLANNER SIDE ALSO NEEDS A CHANGE IS AN OPEN QUESTION FOR RESEARCH, NOT A PRE-COMMITTED EDIT. Stating the obligation in prose is this record's floor. If research finds there is no plan-phase carrier that would actually cause the snapshot to be taken -- so that the prose obligation has no executor -- RAISE IT and say so in the completion summary rather than silently widening this record into a plan-postflight mechanism change. Do NOT change `lean-challenge-snapshot.sh`, its status gate or its exit codes; the gate is correct and is the thing that revealed the defect.

ADDITIONAL ACCEPTANCE FOR ITEM 3:

(10) Item 2's first branch is stated as a plan-phase obligation discharged before the task's status leaves `planned`, NOT as a step an implementation plan schedules; the guidance names exit 73 and the pre-implementation status set so a reader meeting the refusal recognises the defect; it states that a plan scheduling the snapshot as a phase task is defective; and it states that an implementer meeting such a step does not use `--force` and falls back to the declaration-by-declaration diff. If research concluded the prose obligation has no executor on the plan side, that is raised in the completion summary rather than silently absorbed.

### 538. Bounded in-file block edits: index and assert, never string-splice
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: None

**Description**: Add agent-system guidance for the ASSERTION half of a bounded in-file block edit: assert the expected pre-state before writing, and assert an expected post-state invariant immediately after writing, so that a block edit which goes wrong is caught at once instead of being committed. The ANCHOR-SELECTION half of this same failure class is ALREADY CLAIMED by a sibling record in the source-store repository's own task space -- see the sibling-coverage section below. This record must not restate that half, and is not a licence to rewrite it.

MEASURED, NOT HYPOTHESIZED. A python slice-and-splice edit intended only to flip one phase heading marker and tick that phase's checklist items instead DUPLICATED 773 LINES of a plan file: phases 1 through 9 appeared twice in the result. The mechanism was reconstructing the file by concatenating string slices of its own text; an off-target slice boundary silently re-emitted a region that was already present, and nothing in the write path noticed. The intended change was a handful of characters.

HOW IT WAS CAUGHT, AND WHY THAT IS THE POINT. The duplication was detected IMMEDIATELY by a post-edit `grep -n '^### Phase'` showing 18 phase headings where 9 were expected. The defect was not caught by the edit mechanism, by a diff review, or by reading the file -- it was caught by one cheap assertion on a count that the editor knew in advance. That assertion is the whole lesson, and guidance that omits it is not guidance.

HOW IT WAS RECOVERED, AND A NUANCE THE GUIDANCE MUST STATE EXPLICITLY. The file was restored without loss by rewriting it from `git show HEAD:<path>` and then redoing the edit correctly. THAT RECOVERY IS A PLAIN WRITE, NOT A DESTRUCTIVE GIT OPERATION: `git show` reads a blob to stdout and the restore is an ordinary file write, so the destructive-git guard (`guard-destructive-git.sh`) was never involved and no snapshot was required. State this plainly, because an agent that believes recovery from a botched in-file edit requires `git checkout --`, `git restore`, or `git reset --hard` will either escalate for a permission it does not need or reach for an operation that genuinely is guarded and genuinely would discard its other uncommitted work. The safe recovery path for ONE clobbered file is `git show HEAD:<path>` piped to a write, and it is available on a dirty tree with no guard interaction at all.

WHAT A SIBLING RECORD ALREADY COVERS -- READ IT BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING. The source-store repository (~/.config/nvim) maintains its OWN task space, and a record there already covers the anchor-selection half of this failure class: `lean_phase_commit_full_build_and_plan_anchor` (its ITEM 2), file_scope `agent-system/extensions/lean/context/project/lean4/agents/lean-implementation-flow.md`, `agents/lean-implementation-agent.md`, `agents/lean-implementation-hard-agent.md`. Its incident: a plan-file section splice used the bare string '## Lean Challenge Statements' as its END anchor; that same string also occurs earlier in the file's Goals prose, so the splice matched the earlier occurrence and duplicated 752 lines. Its guidance: a section edit anchors on a LINE beginning with the heading markers and searches FORWARD from the target section's start, never on a bare substring that may recur in prose elsewhere. That record ALSO states explicitly that the failure mode may not be lean-specific at all and that a shared home in the core extension is an acceptable outcome of its own planning, with the lean files pointing at it rather than restating it. THIS RECORD THEREFORE OWNS ONLY THE ASSERTION HALF, and must coordinate with that record on the shared home rather than racing it to create one.

WHY THE ASSERTION HALF IS A GENUINELY SEPARATE ADDITION AND NOT A RESTATEMENT -- THE DECIDING MEASUREMENT. Correct anchor selection would not have prevented either incident on its own, and the two incidents' outcomes differ in exactly the way that proves it. The sibling record's 752-line duplication was COMMITTED: commit 83085ed7e in the consumer repository carries the message "mark phase 14 completed in plan" together with a diff of 752 insertions, and it took a FOLLOW-UP commit, f0ef67f81, to restore the file (19 insertions, 771 deletions). The duplication survived the edit, the commit message, and whatever review that commit received. This record's own 773-line duplication, by contrast, never reached a commit at all, because a post-write `grep -n '^### Phase'` count assertion fired immediately. Same failure class, same magnitude, opposite outcome -- and the only difference in the editing procedure was the presence of one cheap assertion on a count known in advance. An anchor rule makes the mistake rarer; the assertion is what makes it loud. Both halves are needed, which is why neither record should absorb the other silently.

THE DISCIPLINE TO RECORD, IN THREE PARTS, THE THIRD BEING THIS RECORD'S OWN. (1) INDEX, DO NOT SPLICE. Address the edit by line index -- read the file into a list of lines, locate the target block's start and end by matching the lines that delimit it, and replace or rewrite only the lines in that range -- rather than computing character offsets into the file's text and concatenating slices around them. (2) BOUND THE RANGE BY AN EXPLICIT TERMINATOR, AND ASSERT THE PRE-STATE. The originating repair bounded the loop by the NEXT TOP-LEVEL SECTION HEADING rather than by a computed length, and asserted that the located range looked as expected before writing anything -- the marker to be flipped was actually present, the checklist items actually matched, the range actually terminated where a terminator was found rather than at end of file. An edit whose pre-state assertion fails must abort without writing, not proceed on a best guess. HOW THE TERMINATOR ITSELF IS CHOSEN belongs to the sibling record named above -- CITE its heading-line-anchored, search-forward rule, do not restate or re-derive it. (3) ASSERT A POST-STATE INVARIANT IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE WRITE. Pick a property of the whole file that the edit must not change and check it in the same breath as the write -- here, the count of `^### Phase` headings. A structural count is the cheapest and most sensitive such invariant for a sectioned document; a total line count is weaker but still catches gross duplication. Part (3) is THIS RECORD'S distinctive contribution and the one no sibling record covers: parts (1) and (2) make the common failure less likely, part (3) is what makes the uncommon one loud instead of silent.

STATE A TRIGGER CONDITION THE READER CAN CHECK BEFORE ACTING. The guidance must not read as a general prohibition that a reader has to interpret. The trigger is conjunctive: the target is a BOUNDED BLOCK inside a larger line-structured text file (a phase inside a plan, a section inside a document, a record inside a log), AND the mechanism under consideration RECONSTRUCTS the file from string slices of its own content rather than replacing identified lines in place. Both halves must hold. Rewriting a whole file from computed content is not this failure class; neither is a line-indexed in-place replacement, which is the prescribed alternative.

NAME THE FIRST-CHOICE MECHANISM, NOT ONLY THE FALLBACK. The harness `Edit` tool with a unique `old_string` is ITSELF a bounded, assert-on-match edit: it fails loudly when the match is absent or ambiguous, which is precisely the pre-state assertion part (2) asks for, obtained for free. It is the first choice for a small bounded edit and the guidance should say so before describing any scripted path. The scripted, line-indexed path earns its place when the edit is repetitive across many sites in one file, or mechanical enough that enumerating `Edit` calls is impractical -- which is exactly the situation the originating incident was in (one heading marker plus a run of checklist items). Guidance that jumps straight to "write a careful python loop" has skipped the cheaper correct answer.

WHAT THE GUIDANCE MUST NOT SAY. Do not generalize this into "do not use python/scripts to edit files", and do not frame it as "always use the Edit tool" -- both are false and both will be ignored once a reader meets a case they do not fit. Do not present the post-state assertion as optional verification that a careful editor may skip; the originating editor WAS being careful and still shipped a 773-line duplication. Do not restate the destructive-git rules; reference `.claude/rules/git-workflow.md` for those and keep this record's git content to the one `git show HEAD:<path>` recovery nuance above.

BOTH AUDIENCES MUST BE REACHED, AND THEY READ DIFFERENT FILES. (i) An IMPLEMENTER performing the edit needs the mechanism and the assertions. (ii) A PLAN AUTHOR must not author a step phrased as a slice-and-splice reconstruction in the first place. The implementer path is the primary one here -- unlike the jq record this is sequenced behind, the originating defect arose in an implementer's own edit mechanism rather than in a plan step -- so `agents/general-implementation-agent.md`, which already points at sibling core patterns, is the natural referrer and is declared in this record's file_scope. State in the plan which path reaches which audience.

SITING -- THREE RECORDS NOW BEAR ON ONE HOME; READ BOTH NEIGHBOURS BEFORE CREATING A FILE. The shared discipline is claimed, in whole or in part, by this record, by the jq-reserialization record this one is sequenced behind, and by the sibling anchor record in the source-store repository's task space. Creating a new pattern file without reading the other two risks a third competing file about one discipline. Resolution order: (i) read the jq record's landed siting decision -- if it created a new sibling pattern file, ADD a section to that file and widen this record's file_scope to it rather than creating `bounded-block-edit.md`; if it extended `jq-escaping-workarounds.md` instead, create the new file declared in file_scope, because neither a Markdown splice nor an assertion discipline belongs inside a file about jq pitfalls. (ii) Read the sibling anchor record's landed state -- if it has already relocated its ITEM 2 guidance into a core-extension home, that home is THIS record's target too and no new file is warranted; if it has not, this record's file becomes the shared home that record invited, and the lean-side files should POINT at it rather than restate it. In EVERY branch the `index-entries.json` entry and at least one referrer are part of THIS change, not a follow-up -- an unreferenced pattern file is not guidance, it is a file.

SCOPE: GUIDANCE ONLY, NO HELPER SCRIPT. Decided at filing time, for the same reasons the predecessor record records for its own case: the proven mechanism is a short line-indexed loop plus two assertions, and the part that is actual work -- knowing which block this edit targets and which invariant must hold for this file -- cannot be factored into a wrapper. A generic "safe block editor" would need its own test suite, deploy registration and maintenance, out of proportion to one minor, already-recovered incident. REOPEN CONDITION, which the guidance itself should name: if the assertion recipe is being retyped across many tasks, revisit the wrapper question then.

NOTHING IN THE REPOSITORY IS BROKEN. The affected plan file was repaired in the originating run and is correct as it stands; do not re-edit it, and do not treat this record as a data-repair record. This record's entire deliverable is prose in the source store plus its wiring.

ACCEPTANCE. (1) The guidance states the conjunctive trigger condition in terms a reader can check before acting, and names at least one concrete file shape that meets it. (2) It carries a copyable recipe covering all three parts -- line indexing, the bounded range with its pre-state assertion, and the post-write invariant assertion -- not merely a prohibition. (3) It names the `Edit`-tool-with-unique-`old_string` path as the first choice and says when the scripted path earns its place instead. THIS IS THE STRONGEST AVAILABLE EVIDENCE FOR THIS RECORD'S OWN THESIS. The duplication was
detected IMMEDIATELY by a post-edit heading grep showing duplicate Phase 2/3 headings -- the
assertion half, exactly as this record argues. Recovery was non-destructive:
`git show HEAD:<path> > <path>`. The edit was then redone with LINE-INDEXED, forward-searched
heading anchors and succeeded. So both halves are now evidenced by two independent incidents each,
and the remedy for the anchor half is specific and known: a plan-marker edit must resolve its
anchors to LINE INDICES of headings, forward-searched from the slice start, never to bare
substring offsets -- which structurally cannot splice backwards.

- **Effort**: low
- **Status**: [NOT STARTED]
- **Task Type**: meta
- **Topic**: agent-system
- **Dependencies**: None

**Description**: lean-implementation-agent's Final Verification Stage step 5 ('Plan compliance spot-check'; source: agent-system/extensions/lean/agents/lean-implementation-agent.md) greps the plan's Goal names ONLY under the roots returned by lean-src-roots.sh (FormalSystem, Tests, BimodalTools; source: agent-system/extensions/lean/scripts/lean-src-roots.sh). Plans following this repository's evidence-probe convention pin their Goals in specs/evidence/**/*.lean, outside those roots. On one such plan the literal check reported 8 of 8 Goals MISSING while a probe-scoped grep found 8 of 8 present at their pinned signatures; the agent recorded both readings in .return-meta.json and set compliance_check from the plan-named location rather than the heuristic's scope. Deliverable: have the spot-check derive its grep scope from the PLAN itself -- the plan's Files-to-modify list, or the Challenge snapshot manifest -- unioned with (not substituted for) the resolved source roots, so both in-tree and probe-scoped Goals are found; apply the same widened scope to the replacement-target sub-check; leave step 0's resolve-or-abort posture and the roots-only consumers elsewhere in the stage (sorry census, axiom and vacuity checks, build) unchanged. A task editing agent-system/extensions/lean/index-entries.json and context/project/lean4/domain/ladder-counter-observables.md in the source store hit a pre-existing uncommitted FOREIGN hunk in the same JSON file (an unrelated line_count bump), and had to hand-stage a HEAD-derived blob carrying only its own edits (git hash-object + git update-index --cacheinfo) and then run plain `git commit` with the session trailer by hand -- bypassing the whole scoped-commit contract (commit-lock mutex serialization, ephemeral-exclusion injection, the V3 degenerate-pathspec gate, the session-trailer convention). Deliverable: EITHER a source-store-aware commit path (e.g. an opt-in --repo-root parameter whose default remains today's BASH_SOURCE-derived resolution so every existing caller is byte-identical, which also forces a decision on where the commit-lock mutex and claim leases live when the committed repo is not the calling repo), OR -- if a second repository root is judged out of scope for that script -- a hunk-scoped staging procedure documented verbatim in the source-store/deploy boundary narrative (.claude/context/standards/source-store-deploy-boundary-narrative.md, source under agent-system/extensions/core/context/standards/) so an agent follows a sanctioned recipe instead of improvising git plumbing.
